1:
Keil and Delitzsch head the chapter as the beginning of the announcement of salvation and take the second half of the book as a whole: in the first half severe judgments had been predicted for the covenant nation and the heathen alike, but Israel was also promised the turning of its captivity, a restoration to its own land, the setting up of the covenant made with the fathers and the renewal of the nation by the Spirit of God, while the kingdoms of the world were threatened with devastation or with lasting humiliation in the nether world. Gill notes that after a run of prophecies against the Ammonites, the Tyrians and the Egyptians a fresh word comes concerning the Jews, and Clarke that the prophet, having addressed other nations, now returns to his own. Henry adds that he had been taken off from prophesying to them when the siege began and is now, two years later with the city taken, appointed to speak to them again; had God abandoned them he would not have sent them prophets.

Henry treats the watchman first as a civil arrangement and the ordinance as a piece of common prudence. It is public danger that occasions the appointment, and the sword of war, however unjustly men draw it, is of God bringing. A country in fear of invasion sets one of its own borderers, a likely man well acquainted with all the avenues of the danger, to be its watchman, in which the children of this world are wise in their generation; and one man may in this way be of public service to a whole country. Princes and statesmen, he adds, are the watchmen of a kingdom. The trust is double: the watchman must discover the approaches of the enemy, and therefore must be neither blind nor asleep, and must give notice of them at once by the trumpet, as a sentinel now does by discharging a gun.

The accounting then runs both ways. If the watchman does his part and the people will not believe the danger to be as great or as near as it is, the blame is not his; and a man who goes presumptuously into the mouth of danger after hearing the trumpet has destroyed himself, and is his own murderer. But if the watchman might have seen the danger and did not, being asleep or heedless or looking another way, or saw it and shifted only for his own safety, the blood of those cut off is required at his hand; and Henry presses that they are cut off suddenly, in their iniquity, without time to repent, which makes the matter worse. Where both do their part, both have delivered their souls. Gill runs the same ground on the side of the people, describing the man who hears the alarm and thinks it a trifle, or reckons the enemy far enough off that there is time yet to prepare.

The application follows. Henry marks one difference: the people of the land set their own watchman, but Israel did not, being less wise for their souls than for their temporal interests, so God appointed one for them. Clarke notices the same asymmetry between this passage and the earlier commission, that here the people choose the watchman and there the Lord appoints him, and remarks that when God chooses the people should approve. Ellicott takes the whole section as the introduction to the renewed commission, closely answering the earlier one, but with a retrospective purpose too, explaining to the people why the prophet had until then spoken so much of judgment and in such warning tones; that had been his duty and would remain so. He adds that the passage is too clear to need comment. Wesley notes only that the man taken away is punished by the Lord for his own sin.
10:
The people speak first, and the voices agree on what they mean. Ellicott sets the reversal sharply: when the prophet warned of impending judgments they refused to believe, and now that the judgments have fallen they despair, asking whether any hope is left if all this is punishment for their sins. Wesley itemises what they had lost, their country wasted, their city burnt and the public worship of God abolished, and puts their conclusion as too late to hope. Clarke feels the weight of it, the sins upon them as a burden too heavy to bear, and answers with the invitation to the heavy laden. Henry finds the sting in a misused text: the prophet had said they would pine away in their iniquities, and they throw it back at him as though it had been spoken absolutely to drive them to despair, when it was spoken conditionally to bring them to repentance.

The answer is put under oath, which Gill takes as showing the certainty and sincerity of it. Henry makes the most of the form: God swears, and since he could swear by no greater he swears by himself, so that we have his word and his oath, two immutable things. It is certain, Henry says, that he has no delight in the ruin of sinners; that the call to turn is sincere, urged and repeated rather than merely commanded, since he not only commands but courts them; and that if sinners perish it is owing to themselves, for they die because they will die. Ellicott states the same doctrine flatly, that the Creator and Father of all can have no pleasure in the death of any, and adds that the verses following reiterate the earlier teaching on individual responsibility before God. Clarke simply refers the reader back to the chapter where the argument was first made.

Their second complaint is against the justice rather than the kindness, that the way of the Lord is not equal, which Henry reads as a charge of partiality and of severity beyond what the case required. Gill is harder on them, noting that they persist after plain proofs to the contrary, and that the speakers are called the children of the prophet people and not the people of God, since the children of God could not say such a thing. Henry answers that the nation as a nation was now dead and ruined, so that the prophet must deal with particular persons, the rule for whom runs much as it does for a nation.

The rule itself is stated in two directions. Gill puts it in a sentence: the righteousness of a man who trusts in it, sinning and not repenting, will not save him, and the wickedness of a repenting sinner will not damn him. Clarke sharpens the first half into a warning against trusting one own performance, of keeping the statutes of religion and the laws of right and wrong between men and committing iniquity notwithstanding. Henry gives it at length: by making bold on the confines of sin a man is drawn at last into the depths, which ruined the Pharisees, who trusted that their long prayers and their fasting twice in the week would atone for devouring widows houses; and one who turns to iniquity and does not return cannot plead his former service, as a rebel cannot plead that he was once a loyal subject. On the other side Henry notices which word does the work, since the assurance of life emboldened the righteous man to sin while the sentence of death quickened the wicked man to return, so that the threatenings of the word may become a savour of life and the promises a savour of death. Gill marks the restored pledge as the evidence of the change, the garment taken from a poor man given back before sunset as the law required.
21:
Henry sets out what happened. The city was burnt in the eleventh year and the fifth month; the news reached the prophet in the twelfth year and the tenth month, a year and almost five months later. He supposes that with a constant correspondence between the two places at that time the prophet must have heard of it long before, but that this was the first account from a refugee, from one who had escaped the flames himself and could be particular and pathetic in the telling, one who could say that he had himself seen those miserable scenes. Wesley glosses the message in two words, that the city was taken and plundered. Clarke fixes the day and adds that this very message had been promised to the prophet in an earlier chapter.

The interval has to be explained, and the voices divide. Clarke reports a variant: against the twelfth year of the received text, seven of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott, one of De Rossi and the Syriac read the eleventh, and though his own copy agrees with the received text he thinks the shorter interval probably genuine. Ellicott defends the twelfth year with a logistical argument. The news itself must have reached Babylon long before, but the prophet was to have it from the mouth of a fugitive with full and circumstantial detail, and there are reasons why that could not have happened earlier: after the capture the general took the mass of the people and the abundant spoil first to the king at Riblah, where some were executed and time was spent settling the affairs of the ruined land, after which the journey of captives carrying heavy spoil was slow and broken by halts. He notes that the returning captives, unhindered, took exactly four months on the same road, so that four times as long is not surprising. Keil and Delitzsch raise the same difficulty of the eleventh year against the twelfth.

What the date fixes, Keil and Delitzsch say, is the precise point at which the earlier promise was fulfilled and the obstacle removed, so that the prophet could speak and prophesy without restraint. Gill describes the impulse: the prophet was under a spirit of prophecy and knew the message before the messenger arrived, so that he was prepared to receive it and to prophesy on it. Ellicott makes the grammar carry the same point, preferring the pluperfect, that the hand of the Lord had already been upon him. Wesley is careful that the prophet had not been wholly dumb before, since he had prophesied against many nations, but had been forbidden to say anything of the Jews; now the Spirit moved him to speak and continued that motion until the messenger came and ever after. Clarke reads the opening of the mouth as vindication, that they now had the fullest evidence he had spoken from the Lord, so that he spoke freely and fully.

Henry draws the same conclusion, that he was no longer dumb and prophesied with more freedom and boldness, being proved a true prophet by the event, to the confusion of those who had contradicted him. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead and note what kind of word came first: not a consoling one but a rebuke, aimed at those who, unrepentant, boasted in the promise of everlasting possession made to the fathers and imagined they might still hold the land after the destruction of the city and the kingdom.
23:
Ellicott identifies the speakers exactly. The poor of the people had been left in the land as vine-dressers and husbandmen, joined by Jews who fled back from Moab and Ammon and elsewhere; and since the murder of the governor and the flight into Egypt have plainly not yet happened, this part of the prophecy is addressed to them. Gill and Wesley describe them as those who came out of their holes or returned from neighbouring countries to take possession of a wasted land, and Gill notes that they were lifted up and haughty about it, as their own words show. Ellicott adds that from this point to the last section of the book none of the prophecies are dated, and that since the closing vision comes more than twelve years later they must have been uttered at intervals across that span, with no means now of fixing them.

Their argument is simple, and everyone states it the same way. Clarke puts it as a question: if Abraham was called to inherit the land when he was alone and had the whole of it to himself, why should not his posterity, who are many, be established in it? Wesley presses the comparison further in their favour, that the promise was made to the seed as well as to the father, and that it is theirs in possession, whereas Abraham had not one foot of it. Ellicott calls the reliance on descent characteristic of the nation in every age, and the same trust in external privilege a standing temptation for anyone whose heart is alienated from God. He traces their retreat from one shelter to the next: first that God would not abandon his city and temple, then that the judgments were too distant to cause alarm, and now, with the warnings all fulfilled, that the land is theirs by promise, the conditions attached to its enjoyment from the first being forgotten.

The answer is a list of charges. Clarke sets the righteousness of Abraham against their unrighteousness and dwells on the eating of flesh with the blood, which he says has been absolutely and for ever forbidden. Ellicott makes the point historically, that the prohibition was given first after the flood and repeatedly under the law, and observes that the crimes charged here are the same alleged all along, another prophet giving a sad picture of their open rebellion. On standing upon the sword, Ellicott denies that war can be meant and takes it of individual crimes of violence; Wesley agrees that they trust their sword and do everything by violence, and reads the abominations as idolatry. Gill notes that they trusted the sword to secure their right to the land.

The sentence closes the oracle. Clarke takes those in the wastes for the Jews who had fled to rocks, caves and mountain strongholds, and reads their death as coming partly by the sword, partly by wild beasts and partly by famine. Ellicott corrects the forts of the English to the natural fastnesses in which the land abounded. Gill takes the doubled word for desolation as one desolating judgment following another until the land is wholly waste. Ellicott closes on the difference from the northern kingdom, whose land was repopulated by colonies from elsewhere because the ten tribes were not to return, whereas Judah was to be left uninhabited so that it might be re-occupied by the returning exiles; and he notes that the complete dispersion, which war and conquest had not accomplished, was finished by the flight of the remnant into Egypt out of fear.
30:
Keil and Delitzsch attach this closing word to the prophet himself and to the whole second half of his ministry, connecting it with the instructions given at his first call. Wesley identifies the speakers as the captives in Babylon, and Ellicott suspects they were not so much those who had been with him all along as fresh captives of a worse character just brought from the ruined city. What they are doing divides the readers. Clarke insists the preposition means concerning rather than against, following two ancient versions, since the verses that follow show the prophet was much respected; and he adds that talking by the walls and in the doorways is no peculiar custom but what idle people and people resting from work do in every country when the weather allows. Ellicott makes the same correction and takes the walls to mean within doors, so that the phrase covers both private and public talk; the people, he says, were not opposed to the prophet but enjoyed his eloquence and talked of him as they met, much as a popular preacher is treated now. Henry reads it darker, as invidious reflections behind his back from those who spoke well to his face, and notes that faithful ministers do not know how much ill is said of them daily, which is as well, since it might discourage them.

The show of attendance is described minutely. Henry lists what was right about them: they came as duly and early as any hearer, to the house of the prophet since there was no temple or synagogue in Babylon; they sat with gravity and composure, none of them whispering or gazing about or sleeping, and sat out the time without wishing the sermon done; they attended to what was said; and they professed a great kindness for him, even a concern that he should not spend himself in preaching or expose himself to the Chaldeans. But their coming as the people came suggests to him that they came because others came, for company and for fashion sake. Ellicott renders the phrase as in crowds and puts the emphasis in the next clause on the pronoun, that they sat as though they were the true people of God while their inward disposition was far otherwise. Gill says they came as early and as constantly and with as much seeming pleasure as any.

The figure of the song draws the fullest comment. Gill takes it of a hearer who regards the voice and the music rather than the matter, delighted with the harmony, the eloquence of the speech, the propriety of the expressions and the cadence of the words, and affected no otherwise than at a concert, or by a singer who can play well on an instrument at the same time and make the two agree. Clarke says they admired the fine voice and correct delivery, that this was their religion, and that it is the whole religion of thousands still, itching ears never having been so multiplied. Henry allows the prophet everything they praised, his surprising matter, fine language, apt similitudes, melodious voice and graceful delivery, and then draws the line: men may have their fancies pleased by the word without having their consciences touched, the itching ear gratified without the corrupt nature sanctified. The love they showed, he says, was only from the teeth outward, their heart going after their covetousness.

The last word turns on them. Clarke and Gill both take the fulfilment as the desolations already threatened by sword and pestilence and wild beasts, and read the recognition as coming too late: when what was predicted arrives, and it is at the doors, they will be convinced that a prophet had been among them by whose ministry they did not profit as they ought.
